gm.road_lines: Yellow Outside - White Inside / Red Outside - White Inside

items.html:
South Africa drives on the left.

NOTE: A handful of other countries also drive on the left. See this infographic for more information.

On most roads, South Africa utilizes single yellow outer lines and white centre lines.

NOTE: The other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia also use single yellow outer lines.

!!Australia practically never uses yellow outer lines.

South Africa occasionally features unique white triple centre lines with 2 solid lines on the outside and a dashed line on the inside.

You may also sometimes encounter another unique triple centre line, consisting of two white lines with one yellow line in the middle. These centre lines are usually found on larger main roads.

NOTE: The only other countries where you will find road lines like these are the other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia.

Generation 2 coverage is quite common in the country.

It can be recognized by the large circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky.

NOTE: On the continent of Africa, Generation 2 is only found in South Africa.

South Africa has 11 official languages: English, Afrikaans, and various Bantu languages. English is the lingua franca and therefore appears most often on signage.

Afrikaans is a Germanic language that is closely related to Dutch. Common Afrikaans place name suffixes are -fontein, -kraal, -kop, -dorp, -nek, and -berg or -burg. While Afrikaans is most commonly spoken in the western half of the country, you will find Afrikaans place names all over South Africa, meaning that it is not useful for region-guessing.

NOTE: Afrikaans is rare to non-existent in Eswatini and Lesotho. It is also abundantly rare in Botswana, but has some limited presence in the form of place names.

The most common type of pole in South Africa features 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators that resemble rows of birds, which is why they are referred to as “bird poles” in the community.

NOTE: South Africa has a wide variety of other poles and pole tops. Some of these are (mostly) limited to a certain region; you can learn more about them in the region guessing section.

South Africa uses green directional signs with the road number in yellow.

NOTE: Green directional signs with yellow road numbers are also used in Lesotho, Eswatini, Botswana and Namibia. Here, the format of road numbers is useful:

  • !!N and R-roads are exclusive to South Africa.
  • !!A and B-roads are exclusive to Botswana, Lesotho and Namibia. In addition to this, Namibia uses C, D, M and F roads.
  • !!MR-roads are exclusive to Eswatini.

South Africa utilizes triangular warning signs with a red border and a white background.

NOTE: The four other southern African countries use similar warning signs.

!!Australia and New Zealand use yellow diamond-shaped warning signs.

South Africa uses white-and-red chevrons. You can find a similar chevron pattern below directional signs.

In addition, unique-looking small, thin chevrons with one arrow are common next to roads.

NOTE: The thin chevrons can also be found in the other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia.
Suburban houses in and around large cities will often be surrounded by high walls, fences, and gates to deter criminals.

All Generation 4 coverage in South Africa was taken by a blue Street View car with a short antenna.

NOTE: The antenna is sometimes hidden by the blur.

South Africa also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, but with a short antenna on the back.

Each province features a different licence plate design, which can be somewhat visible through the blur. Most notably Free State or KwaZulu-Natal, which have a slight green tint and blue tint respectively.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

A map of major highways in South Africa. On road signs, the letter ‘N’ should appear in front of the highway number. On Google Maps, however, the letter ‘N’ will not be present. Instead, a blue pentagon with the number will be displayed.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Most of the R-roads with three-digit road numbers are geographically grouped. However, many roads go through multiple provinces and some, especially the 100s, are spread throughout the whole country. The map shows roughly where you can find each set of R-roads.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Telephone numbers are 10 digits long. The first three digits of landline numbers are the area code. The first digit is always a zero; the second and third digits give you the area. The area codes are geographically grouped, so even learning just the first digit is useful.

NOTE: Mobile phone numbers start with 06–08. These numbers are not specific to an area.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

_Image provided by dbldk._

Poles with 3 bars forming the letter ‘A’, with the bottom insulators being attached at the edges of a horizontal bar, can be found almost exclusively in Western Cape, and rarely in bordering provinces.
A similar poletop can be found in Eastern Cape, however the A-shape is noticeably wider and the bottom insulators are attached directly to the ‘A’ rather than a horizontal bar.
Trident pole tops are almost unique to KwaZulu-Natal.

Poles with 3 alternating insulators sticking out horizontally at the top are mostly seen in the four northern provinces of Limpopo, Gauteng, North West and Mpumalanga. They can also sometimes be found in Northern Cape. In the rest of the country, these pole tops are exceedingly rare.
Poles with 2 diagonal bars forming a ‘<’ shape can be found mostly in the northeastern provinces, most commonly in Limpopo and North West.
Poles with 1 or 2 metal arms holding up insulators are most commonly seen in Mpumalanga.

Square, red stickers on the back of regular signs are often found in Eastern cape and close to Eastern cape in Northern Cape and Free State. You may see them in the North West province as well, but to a lesser extent.

NOTE: Red stickers on the back of chevrons can be seen in almost every province.
White stickers on the back of chevrons are often seen in the Cape provinces.
You can find this grainy, almost Texas-like pavement with a hint of pink in Limpopo.
Big bird nests on top of poles are commonly seen in the northern part of the Northern Cape Province.
Power plants are often seen in between the town of Secunda and eMalahleni in Mpumalanga.

The northeast of the country can look very dry and somewhat barren, with a lot of orange or red soil. You will often see hills or mountains covered in shrubs.

NOTE: Depending on the season, the coverage can change drastically from dry to very green.

Unique rocky, treeless mountains can be seen in Western Cape, with most of the mountains having tall, steep sides and sharp peaks.

NOTE: Similar mountains can be seen in and around Lesotho.
Vineyards are almost exclusively found in Western Cape, mostly in valleys near the coast. You can also commonly find them near Upington, in Northern Cape.

A dry landscape with red soil is typically found in the Northern Cape.

NOTE: This map is a useful guide in guessing based on the climate of South Africa.
Sugarcane plantations are most commonly seen in KwaZulu-Natal, mostly along the coast. However, they can also be seen in Mpumalanga on the Mozambique border. For an overview, see this map.

Uniquely tall Cook pine trees are found mostly between the cities of East London and Durban along the southeastern coast.

NOTE: These are planted and not native, so they can be found anywhere along the coast.

Tree plantations that consist mostly of pine are common to the west of Eswatini, and some to the south in KwaZulu-Natal.

NOTE: Pine tree plantations are typically seen within the country of Eswatini itself.
Grassy rolling hills are generally located in the coastal area of Western Cape between Cape Town and George, and just north of Cape Town. Tall ridges are usually visible to the north or east.
The landscape near the Mozambique border in the highlighted area is noticeably flat, with green subtropical vegetation.

A camouflage car with black side mirrors and roof racks can be seen in Kruger National Park, on the Mozambique border.

NOTE: The Park now also has generation 4 coverage.

The landscape around Kruger National Park is generally flat, with a savannah climate and dry vegetation. You will not see any agriculture and the vegetation is mostly made up of grasses, with small trees dotting the landscape. Red soil can also be seen below the grass.

In addition, this distinctive directional waystone is commonly found at many junctions.

NOTE: Within the coverage of the park, you will mostly find unpaved gravel roads or small and paved roads without road lines.

Metropolitan Routes are major roads around cities. They are designated with the letter M.

These distinct and unique M route signs are commonly found in Port Elizabeth (Gqeberha) and Durban, respectively.
Traffic lights and pedestrian crossing poles in Johannesburg are encircled by three strips of reflective tape.
While this lamp and arm can be found uncommonly across the country, Durban uniquely has this bump on the top. You may, however, still see the standard lamp and arm.
Poles or any public infrastructure will often be plastered with dodgy adverts for abortion services or penis enlargement pills in and around Gauteng, in particular in Johannesburg and Emalahleni.

The section of the R360 north of Bokspits, next to the Botswana border, has asphalt with a recognizable reddish tint. The landscape is arid and features dry greyish trees, shrubs and long golden grass. The road runs in a general north to south direction.

NOTE: Asphalt with a reddish tint can be found on other roads and the southern part of the R360. However, the landscape north of Bokspits looks predominantly like this.
The distinct Table Mountain, located west of Cape Town, can be recognized by its prominent three-kilometre plateau. It is flanked by Devil’s Peak, which is more pyramidal.
Mountains in the Witfontein Nature Reserve, likely George’s Peak, will be visible north from the city of George.

lm.name: South Africa
lm.note:
Telephone numbers are 10 digits long. The first three digits of landline numbers are the area code. The first digit is always a zero; the second and third digits give you the area. The area codes are geographically grouped, so even learning just the first digit is useful.

NOTE: Mobile phone numbers start with 06–08. These numbers are not specific to an area.

lm.name: Alternating Insulator Pole
lm.note: This pole top with 3 alternating short insulators is most common in the North-East of the country, but is also occasionally found in Northern Cape. They can also very rarely be found elsewhere in the country but infrequently enough to hedge north-east if nothing contradicts it.

lm.name: Area Code - 011
lm.note:
011 should put you in or very close to Johannesburg.

Other 01X numbers should put you in the general North-East of the country. See the map for more info.

lm.name: Area Code - 012
lm.note:
012 should put you in or very close to Pretoria.

Other 01X numbers should put you in the general North-East of the country. See the map for more info.

lm.name: Area Code - 01X
lm.note:
01X numbers should put you in the general North-East of the country (including Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and most of North West). Knowing which area of the country you are in from the first digit of the area code is helpful to know.

See the map for more info if you want to know area codes in further detail.

lm.name: Area Code - 021
lm.note:
021 should put you in or very close to Cape Town.

Other 02X numbers should put you in the general West of the country. See the map for more info.

lm.name: Area Code - 02X
lm.note:
02X numbers should put you in the general West of the country (including Western Cape minus the area around George and west Northern Cape). Knowing which area of the country you are in from the first digit of the area code is helpful to know.

See the map for more info if you want to know area codes in further detail.

lm.name: Area Code - 031
lm.note:
031 should put you in or very close to Durban.

Other 03X numbers should put you in the general South-East of the country. See the map for more info.

lm.name: Area Code - 03X
lm.note:
03X numbers should put you in the general South-East of the country (including KwaZulu-Natal and far east parts of Eastern Cape). Knowing which area of the country you are in from the first digit of the area code is helpful to know.

See the map for more info if you want to know area codes in further detail.

lm.name: Area Code - 041
lm.note:
041 should put you in or very close to Gqeherba.

Other 04X numbers should put you in the general South of the country. See the map for more info.

lm.name: Area Code - 04X
lm.note:
04X numbers should put you in the general South of the country (including Eastern Cape and the area around George in Western Cape). Knowing which area of the country you are in from the first digit of the area code is helpful to know.

See the map for more info if you want to know area codes in further detail.

lm.name: Area Code - 051
lm.note:
051 should put you in or close to Bloemfontein.

Other 05X numbers should put you in the general Centre or North-West of the country. See the map for more info.

lm.name: Area Code - 05X
lm.note:
05X numbers should put you in the general Centre or North-West of the country (including Free State, western North West and east+central Northern Cape). Knowing which area of the country you are in from the first digit of the area code is helpful to know.

See the map for more info if you want to know area codes in further detail.

lm.name: Bird Nest Pole
lm.note: Some electricity poles in sections of Northern Cape can have bird nests on them. These can either be large nests covering the entire pole top, or more rarely be smaller nests visible on a part of the pole top. The bigger ones are often visible quite far away.

lm.name: Eastern Cape License Plate
lm.note: Eastern Cape license plates can be spotted through blur with a yellow section on top of a green section left of the centre of the plate, combined with white either side of this pattern. These are most similar to North West plates, but their plates have a green blur visible along the entire bottom of the plate instead of just below the yellow part. A yellow/green on the very right of the plate can sometimes be seen too.

lm.name: Johannesburg Traffic Lights
lm.note: Traffic lights in Johannesburg have three lines of reflective tape on them. This isn't found anywhere else in the country.

lm.name: Kruger Park Google Car
lm.note: Kruger National Park in the north-east of the country uses a unique Google car not found anywhere else in the world. The car looks like a standard roof-rack car but the front of the car has a camoflague pattern. Some of the coverage (mostly the main roads) has been overwritten by Gen 4 coverage though, so you can still get a round here that doesn't have this unique car.

lm.name: North West License Plate
lm.note: North West license plates can be spotted through blur with a thin green line across the bottom and 1 or 2 sections of yellow on the left half of the plate. These are most similar to Free State plates, but their plates often have more green visible through blur and the yellow section is more often visible on the right of Free State plates rather than the left.

lm.name: Northern Cape License Plate
lm.note: Northern Cape license plates can be spotted through blur with either a yellow section across the right-most 2/3 of the plate, or a G-Y-G-Y-G pattern due to the green letters of the plate. These are most similar to Free State plates, but Free State plates should have more green visible through the blur.

lm.name: Pine Tree Plantations
lm.note: Pine tree plantations are mostly found in KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumulanga. It is possible to be driving through them, see them from a distance, or both. Neighbouring Eswatini also has a lot of these so make sure you know what country you are in. One easy way to tell is Eswatini only has Gen 3 camera coverage with a white google car, whereas South Africa will often have Gen 4 camera coverage with a blue car, or Gen 2 camera coverage.

lm.name: Rocky Mountains
lm.note: Mountains that are predominantly rocky with very little or no vegetation are most common in Western Cape. The mountains here are often tall with steep sides rather than gradual slopes, and the mountains are often closer to the camera than mountains found elsewhere in the country.

lm.name: Standard A-Shape Pole
lm.note: This A-shaped pole top with all 3 insulators being vertical is almost exclusive to Western Cape. It shows up often in the state which makes it one of the most crucial pole tops to remember.

lm.name: Sugarcane Plantations
lm.note: Sugarcane plantations are mostly found in KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumulanga. These are especially common around the Durban area and near Eswatini.

lm.name: Triangle/Diagonal Pole
lm.note: This diagonal or triangle pole top is most common in North West and Limpopo, but is also seen regularly in Mpumalanga and sometimes in Gauteng and Free State.

lm.name: Trident Pole
lm.note: This trident pole top is almost exclusive to KwaZulu-Natal. It shows up often in the state which makes it one of the most crucial pole tops to remember.

lm.name: Vineyards
lm.note: Vineyards are found in very few places other than Western Cape. The vineyards can be seen in different seasons so it is important to recognize what they look like in both summer coverage and winter coverage. In summer, they will look like the picture below. In winter, they will lose their leaves but the vines will still be in neat rows.

lm.name: Wide A-Shape Pole
lm.note: This A-shaped pole top with the bottom insulators being horizontal is almost exclusive to Eastern Cape. This pole top does not show up too often but should be reliable when it does.

lm.name: Yellow Outer Lines
lm.note:
In South Africa, most paved roads have single yellow outer lines and white center lines. This can be used to differentiate from Australia which has only white lines and never single yellow lines.

REMEMBER:

  • The Middle East can also have single yellow outer lines, so use driving side to tell them apart (South Africa drives left)
  • Botswana, Eswatini and Lesotho also use single yellow outer lines (but they usually have a white car)

lm.name: Bird nests pole top
lm.note: Big bird nests on top of poles are commonly seen in the northern part of the Northern Cape Province.

lm.name: Blue back of google car(GEN4)
lm.note:
If you see blue back of the google car with/or without antenna you can be only in South Africa or Europe.

With yellow outer lines and driving left you are gonna be only in South Africa.

lm.name: KwaZulu trident pole top
lm.note: Trident pole tops are almost unique to KwaZulu-Natal.

lm.name: WC pole top
lm.note: Poles with 3 bars forming the letter ‘A’, with the bottom insulators being attached at the edges of a horizontal bar, can be found almost exclusively in Western Cape, and rarely in bordering provinces.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• On most roads, South Africa utilizes single yellow outer lines and white centre lines.

--- NOTE:

  • The other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, and Lesotho also use single yellow outer lines.

lm.name: Roadlines #2
lm.note:
• South Africa occasionally features unique white triple centre lines with 2 solid lines on the outside and a dashed line on the inside.
  • You may also sometimes encounter another unique triple centre line, consisting of two white lines with one yellow line in the middle.
  • These centre lines are usually found on larger main roads.

lm.name: 1 or 2 metal arms
lm.note: Poles with 1 or 2 metal arms holding up insulators are most commonly seen in Mpumalanga.

lm.name: 2 diagonal bars
lm.note: Poles with 2 diagonal bars forming a ‘<’ shape can be found mostly in the northeastern provinces, most commonly in Limpopo and North West.

lm.name: 3 alternating insulators
lm.note: Poles with 3 alternating insulators sticking out horizontally at the top are mostly seen in the four northern provinces of Limpopo, Gauteng, North West and Mpumalanga. They can also sometimes be found in Northern Cape. In the rest of the country, these pole tops are exceedingly rare.

lm.name: A poletop
lm.note: Poles with 3 bars forming the letter ‘A’, with the bottom insulators being attached at the edges of a horizontal bar, can be found almost exclusively in Western Cape, and rarely in bordering provinces.

lm.name: bird pole
lm.note: The most common type of pole in South Africa features 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators that resemble rows of birds, which is why they are referred to as “bird poles” in the community.

lm.name: Trident Pole
lm.note: Trident pole tops are almost unique to KwaZulu-Natal.

lm.name: wide A poletop
lm.note: A similar poletop can be found in Eastern Cape, however the A-shape is noticeably wider and the bottom insulators are attached directly to the ‘A’ rather than a horizontal bar.

top.html:
South Africa drives on the left.

NOTE: A handful of other countries also drive on the left. See this infographic for more information.
top.raw: South Africa drives on the **left.** NOTE: A handful of other countries also drive on the left. See [this](/images/south-africa/rightleftdrive.png) infographic for more information.

top.html:
On most roads, South Africa utilizes single yellow outer lines and white centre lines.

NOTE: The other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia also use single yellow outer lines.

!!Australia practically never uses yellow outer lines.
top.raw: On most roads, South Africa utilizes single **yellow outer lines **and white centre lines. NOTE: The other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia also use single yellow outer lines. !!Australia practically never uses yellow outer lines.

top.html:
South Africa occasionally features unique white triple centre lines with 2 solid lines on the outside and a dashed line on the inside.

You may also sometimes encounter another unique triple centre line, consisting of two white lines with one yellow line in the middle. These centre lines are usually found on larger main roads.

NOTE: The only other countries where you will find road lines like these are the other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia.
top.raw: South Africa occasionally features unique white **triple centre lines** with 2 solid lines on the outside and a dashed line on the inside. You may also sometimes encounter another unique triple centre line, consisting of two white lines with one yellow line in the middle. These centre lines are usually found on larger main roads. NOTE: The only other countries where you will find road lines like these are the other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia.

top.html:
Generation 2 coverage is quite common in the country.

It can be recognized by the large circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky.

NOTE: On the continent of Africa, Generation 2 is only found in South Africa.
top.raw: **Generation 2 coverage** is quite common in the country. It can be recognized by the large circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky. NOTE: On the continent of Africa, Generation 2 is only found in South Africa.

top.html:
South Africa has 11 official languages: English, Afrikaans, and various Bantu languages. English is the lingua franca and therefore appears most often on signage.

Afrikaans is a Germanic language that is closely related to Dutch. Common Afrikaans place name suffixes are -fontein, -kraal, -kop, -dorp, -nek, and -berg or -burg. While Afrikaans is most commonly spoken in the western half of the country, you will find Afrikaans place names all over South Africa, meaning that it is not useful for region-guessing.

NOTE: Afrikaans is rare to non-existent in Eswatini and Lesotho. It is also abundantly rare in Botswana, but has some limited presence in the form of place names.
top.raw: South Africa has **11 official languages**: English, Afrikaans, and various Bantu languages. English is the [lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua_franca) and therefore appears most often on signage. **Afrikaans** is a Germanic language that is closely related to Dutch. Common Afrikaans place name suffixes are -fontein, -kraal, -kop, -dorp, -nek, and -berg or -burg. While Afrikaans is most commonly spoken in the [western half](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/16/South_Africa_2011_Afrikaans_speakers_proportion_map.svg) of the country, you will find Afrikaans place names all over South Africa, meaning that it is not useful for region-guessing. NOTE: Afrikaans is rare to non-existent in Eswatini and Lesotho. It is also abundantly rare in Botswana, but has some limited presence in the form of place names.

top.html:
The most common type of pole in South Africa features 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators that resemble rows of birds, which is why they are referred to as “bird poles” in the community.

NOTE: South Africa has a wide variety of other poles and pole tops. Some of these are (mostly) limited to a certain region; you can learn more about them in the region guessing section.
top.raw: The most common type of pole in South Africa features 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators that resemble rows of birds, which is why they are referred to as “**bird poles**” in the community. NOTE: South Africa has a wide variety of other poles and pole tops. Some of these are (mostly) limited to a certain region; you can learn more about them in the region guessing section.

top.html:
South Africa uses green directional signs with the road number in yellow.

NOTE: Green directional signs with yellow road numbers are also used in Lesotho, Eswatini, Botswana and Namibia. Here, the format of road numbers is useful:

  • !!N and R-roads are exclusive to South Africa.
  • !!A and B-roads are exclusive to Botswana, Lesotho and Namibia. In addition to this, Namibia uses C, D, M and F roads.
  • !!MR-roads are exclusive to Eswatini.
top.raw: South Africa uses **green** directional signs with the road number in yellow. NOTE: Green directional signs with yellow road numbers are also used in Lesotho, Eswatini, Botswana and Namibia. Here, the format of road numbers is useful: - !!N and R-roads are exclusive to South Africa. - !!A and B-roads are exclusive to Botswana, Lesotho and Namibia. In addition to this, Namibia uses C, D, M and F roads. - !!MR-roads are exclusive to Eswatini.

top.html:
South Africa utilizes triangular warning signs with a red border and a white background.

NOTE: The four other southern African countries use similar warning signs.

!!Australia and New Zealand use yellow diamond-shaped warning signs.
top.raw: South Africa utilizes **triangular warning signs** with a red border and a white background. NOTE: The four other southern African countries use similar warning signs. !!Australia and New Zealand use yellow diamond-shaped warning signs.

top.html:
South Africa uses white-and-red chevrons. You can find a similar chevron pattern below directional signs.

In addition, unique-looking small, thin chevrons with one arrow are common next to roads.

NOTE: The thin chevrons can also be found in the other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia.
top.raw: South Africa uses **white-and-red **chevrons. You can find a similar chevron pattern below directional signs. In addition, unique-looking [small, thin chevrons](https://goo.gl/maps/UtnQqFLqBe9EupxC6) with one arrow are common next to roads. NOTE: The thin chevrons can also be found in the other southern African countries of Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia.

top.html: Suburban houses in and around large cities will often be surrounded by high walls, fences, and gates to deter criminals.
top.raw: Suburban houses in and around large cities will often be surrounded by **high walls,** fences, and gates** **to deter criminals.

top.html:
All Generation 4 coverage in South Africa was taken by a blue Street View car with a short antenna.

NOTE: The antenna is sometimes hidden by the blur.
top.raw: All Generation 4 coverage in South Africa was taken by a blue Street View car with a short antenna. NOTE: The antenna is sometimes [hidden by the blur](https://maps.app.goo.gl/fKdBXrspbEe8CeaF9).

top.html: South Africa also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, but with a short antenna on the back.
top.raw: South Africa also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, but with a short antenna on the back.
